newsitem.title: USA: Albright sees advance in Indo-Pakistan ties.
newsitem.headline: Albright sees advance in Indo-Pakistan ties.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, encouraged by improved ties between India and Pakistan, said on Tuesday she was considering a trip to the region that would be the first such visit in 14 years.
Albright, speaking to reporters before talks with Pakistani Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan, gave no dates for such a trip, nor did she say which countries she might visit.
"I am considering a trip to the region. This is the 50th anniversary of independence and it seems to be an appropriate time for a trip to be planned," Albright said.

British India was divided into mainly Hindu India and mainly Moslem Pakistan when Britain's colonial rulers withdrew in August 1947. The eastern part of Pakistan later became the separate country of Bangladesh.

U.S. officials said any trip would have to take in at least India and Pakistan. The last U.S. secretary of state to visit both countries was George Shultz in 1983. Shultz also paid a short visit to Pakistan in 1988 to attend the funeral of President Zia ul-Haq.

In a 45-minute meeting, Khan briefed Albright on the outcome of an Indo-Pakistani summit in the Maldives last week, a meeting that she said had been "very important and useful" in improving the two countries' tense relations.

"The secretary was very encouraged by the positive report that she heard," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns. "The United States hopes that this progress between Delhi and Islamabad will continue. We very much support it."

India and Pakistan have fought two wars over Kashmir, of which India rules two-thirds and Pakistan one-third. Albright said a dialogue between the countries on Kashmir "would be very useful and would be terrific to resolve this".
Khan said that the two countries' foreign secretaries planned to meet June 19-22 in Islamabad.

Albright noted that her father had worked on the Kashmir issue as a Czechoslovak diplomat in 1948 and had written a book on the subject. "It would give me great pleasure if that somehow could be resolved at this stage," she said.

U.S. officials signalled no breakthrough in a seven-year deadlock over Pakistan's $658 million purchase of U.S. F-16 fighters, delivery of which was blocked in 1990 because of suspicions over Pakistan's nuclear programme.

Khan listed four ways to resolve the issue. The United States could deliver the aircraft, refund the money or sell the planes to a third country and then reimburse Pakistan. The fourth option, he said, was legal action in U.S. courts.
Burns dismissed the likelihood that Pakistan would go to court, and said Washington remained committed to selling the planes to another country.

But he admitted that a plan to sell the fighters to Indonesia was on hold for now because "conditions haven't been right" in the U.S. Congress to go ahead. Many members of Congress are concerned about Indonesia's human rights record.

Khan indicated that former Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, subpoenaed to appear before a U.S. grand jury in a fund- raising abuse case dating from the 1996 U.S. elections, would be questioned in Pakistan and not come to the United States.

"Benazir Bhutto is now in Islamabad. I understand through the American embassy arrangements are being made to interview her and the other officials, which has nothing to do with the government of Pakistan," Khan told reporters.

A U.S. Justice Department task force wants to question Bhutto about alleged efforts by Representative Dan Burton, an Indiana Republican, to pressure a lobbyist for her government to raise campaign contributions for him, the Washington Post reported on Saturday.
